author: Claude (EFL materials writer role), v2 against the quality gate
basis: Rewritten against the v2 quality gate and the grammatical-range check. A2 and B1 were one text with synonyms swapped (vocabulary overlap 0.63, against a ceiling of 0.34 on average), and the B2 climbed by vocabulary rather than by structure, so each slide was re-conceived at each level - the same fact approached from a different angle with different content words - instead of paraphrased down or up. Every fact, name and number of the source is kept (2030 on slide 19 is the mission's only number). Facts corrected, with the reason: slide 3, the workbook B2's 'Margaining either group' is not a word, read as 'marginalising' and written so; slide 7, 'statistics confirm that professional female athletes receive significantly lower remuneration and prize money than male counterparts for identical performance' is overstated as a blanket claim, because several major tournaments now pay equal prize money, so the line keeps the gap but adds that some competitions have moved to equal prizes while the training week is identical; slide 12, 'remaining silent means compliance' is the wrong word (complicity) and a slogan, replaced by the consequence - silence leaves the player to absorb the abuse alone; slide 13, 'finally granting women's tournaments the expansive global audience they rightfully deserve and can monetize' presents an unfinished shift as complete, hedged to competitions beginning to attract serious sponsors; slide 16, 'sports equity directly correlates with robust macroeconomic stability' and 'legal guarantees of inclusion inevitably maximize a nation's complete human capital' hedged to money spent on women's sport tending to repay itself, with the evidence noted as younger than the claim; slide 5, 'stifles cognitive and physical confidence' reduced to confidence in physical strength, which is what the source's own A2 and B1 lines say; slide 9, careers 'cut short' hedged; slide 10, peers 'evaluated solely on merit' de-absolutised; slide 18, the B2's 'ensuring my media consumption reflects compromising equity' is both a typo (presumably 'uncompromising') and unfalsifiable, replaced by a checkable promise - follow one team, pay for the subscription, discuss the fixtures; slide 19, 'build a truly fair sports world by 2030' reframed as the deadline the agenda names and how much closer we can pull it; slide 20, 'Thank you for listening' removed under the house rule that the speech ends on the claim, and 'Let us exit this hall' rewritten. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count. A2 keeps one clause per sentence, present and past simple and no participle clauses, and carries the argument in concrete everyday words.

slides.1: Hello everyone. Today we look at SDG 5, gender equality, inside the world of sport. Sport teaches us teamwork and fair rules, so every player needs a chance.
slides.2: Why does sport matter here? Sport is a mirror of our society. When millions of girls see women win on television, they learn that talent counts, not gender.
slides.3: Think about the Olympic Games. A country feels proud when its men and its women both win. If we help only one team, we lose half of our national talent.
slides.4: In the past, sport was only for men. People always said that women were too weak to run a marathon or play football. That idea closed the door for decades.
slides.5: These ideas arrive very early. Adults tell boys to run outside and play rough games. They tell girls to sit quietly, so girls slowly stop trusting their own strength.
slides.6: Look at any school playground. The boys usually take the big football field, and the girls get a small corner. Slowly, the girls decide that sport is not for them.
slides.7: Now look at the prize money. In many sports, women still win much smaller prizes, but some big tournaments now pay the champions equally. Women train exactly as hard.
slides.8: Now look at the coaches. Most coaches, team managers and referees are still men. When no women sit at the table, nobody asks about women's health.
slides.9: Many athletes also work at home. They cook, they clean, they care for their family, and then they start training. Their career can end early because nobody helps at home.
slides.10: Change starts with the words we use every day. We should stop using "you play like a girl" as an insult. Say something kind instead, and everybody keeps playing.
slides.11: At school we can share the equipment. Boys and girls can use the same courts and play in mixed teams. Good teamwork teaches us to respect real ability, not gender.
slides.12: Do you hear a joke about a female player? Then say something quickly, before the playground decides it is funny. One calm voice can change the game today.
slides.13: Here is some good news. You can now watch women's basketball, tennis and football on the internet. That window used to be closed, but now it is open.
slides.14: Sports science helps too. Many players now wear a small tracker on the wrist. This technology counts every heart beat, so they can train safely and improve every week.
slides.15: Look at your phone again. Famous players share their training videos there every day. Their stories reach millions of young fans, so share the good ones.
slides.16: Laws are moving as well. Several countries now pay their national teams the same money for women and men. Governments do this because it is good for the country too.
slides.17: Let's look back for a moment. Equality in sport touches our schools, our jobs and our homes. It is a real goal, so let's support female players, coaches and reporters.
slides.18: Here is my promise. I will watch a women's game every month, and I will cheer for my favourite team. So what is your small action today?
slides.19: Change like this takes time and patience. The goals give us one date, and that date is 2030. Let's be the people who make equal play normal.
slides.20: SDG 5 is a mission for you and for me. When the playing field is equal, every team becomes stronger. That is the game I really want to play.
